entries.test: A sustained collapse in AI investment, financing and valuations would establish the predicted bursting of the AI bubble.
entries.note: The eventual collapse is asserted as a premise of the announced series.

entries.test: Financial results of AI businesses and actual data center completion schedules compared with announced schedules would test the claim.
entries.note: The economic claim is sweeping but has a plain profitability reading.

entries.test: AI startups' annual financial results would show whether all lose millions or billions, with a profitable startup providing a counterexample.
Reported investments, announced capex plans and financial break-even calculations would test the asserted revenue requirements.
entries.note: This asserts a present financial requirement based on planned spending, rather than predicting those revenues.

entries.test: The four companies' disclosures through publication would show whether any reported realized AI revenue rather than annualized run rates.
Microsoft's capex records and public testimony about OpenAI infrastructure spending would establish the amount and share since FY2023.
Microsoft capacity disclosures and infrastructure records would show the share of its operational capacity devoted to OpenAI.
entries.note: The proposition adds an AI-only restriction absent from the source's claim about Microsoft's operational capacity.

entries.test: Copilot subscriber counts, subscription prices and discount disclosures would establish its annual revenue ceiling and whether realized revenue falls below it.
Microsoft's FY2025 financial records and OpenAI partnership disclosures would establish inference revenue, revenue sharing and capex.
entries.note: The source counts both spent and allocated capex.
The proposition omits the explicit 10% quarter-over-quarter growth assumption. The source says 'likely.'

entries.test: The accounting definitions and supporting disclosures for the cited capex figures would show whether operating expenses are excluded.
Public GPU service revenues and fully allocated acquisition, financing and operating costs would establish profitability.
entries.note: His own parenthetical disagreement endorses the negative claim despite the surrounding quotation.

entries.test: Realized AI investment returns alongside revenue growth, capex and GPU margins would show whether investment pays off without all four stated conditions.
entries.note: The next sentence allows continuing capex with sufficiently large revenue growth, creating tension with the asserted necessary conditions.

entries.test: Meta's capex guidance and disclosures of revenue attributable to AI through publication would test both assertions.

entries.note: An inability to find a scenario is a report of his own assessment, not a categorical prediction that no such scenario exists.

entries.test: Each company's reported 2023 and 2024 annual capex can be compared directly with $45 billion.
entries.note: The zero-expense assumption makes this an arithmetic comparison, not an inaccessible counterfactual.

entries.test: Hyperscaler AI revenue trajectories and eventual unrecovered costs or write-downs on early infrastructure would test the predicted hundreds of billions in waste.
entries.note: 'Extremely soon' supplies no definite deadline.

entries.test: Compute allocation disclosures and announced investments would establish the labs' capacity share and three-year funding total.
entries.note: The proposition extracts two assertions without retaining the separate conditional future funding detail.

entries.test: Public AI revenue growth figures excluding OpenAI and Anthropic compute purchases would show whether substantial growth was evident at publication.
Microsoft's quarterly RPO disclosures minus the disclosed contributions of OpenAI and Anthropic commitments would establish the residual change.
entries.note: This is an accounting subtraction, not a speculative alternative history.

entries.test: Customer-level AI revenue growth and financing agreements would test growth outside the two labs and whether their purchases require hyperscaler funding.
entries.note: The proposition removes 'do not appear,' strengthening the claim.

entries.test: AI revenues and investment recovery through May 2027 would show whether each company needed more than $100 billion in AI revenue to cover the cited investments.
entries.note: The one-year horizon runs from the May 2026 publication date.
Standing alone, 'too expensive' is an evaluative judgment without a specified economic threshold.
The inference rests on a counterfactual about what companies would disclose if their results were good.

entries.test: LLM providers' operating costs and revenues over time would show whether costs scale approximately linearly with revenue.
entries.note: The linear-scaling assertion supplies a testable component despite the evaluative opening.

entries.test: Hyperscaler capex disclosures and commissioned infrastructure inventories would establish what share of spending had produced operational GPU capacity.
entries.note: The proposition drops the explicit qualification that this is his estimate.

entries.test: AI infrastructure utilization, the labs' financial results and their publicly stated plans would test capacity concentration, losses and an apparent route to ending them.
entries.note: In context, 'said capacity' refers to the operational AI capacity discussed immediately before.

entries.test: Documented recovery of AI investments without a major new product line or three to four additional lab-sized compute contracts would falsify the claim.

entries.note: 'May die' expresses a possibility.
He explicitly frames this as a speculative 'chaos bet' and repeatedly disclaims knowledge.
The source lists requirements and expresses doubt about margins. The proposition turns the sarcastically tentative completion date into a distinct delay prediction.

entries.test: Public inference revenue and cost disclosures would establish whether evidence of profitable inference exists and whether evidence supports losses.
Subscription entitlements, measured usage and disclosed inference costs would test the stated consumption ratio and inference profitability.
entries.note: The source does not specify that the $8–$13.50 figure measures actual compute cost rather than usage valued at token prices.

entries.test: The labs' cash-flow results and documented financial plans would show their losses and whether a financially viable route to sustainability exists.
entries.note: The closing exception merely restates that sustainability requires ending cash burn.

entries.test: Anthropic's and OpenAI's financial results would establish whether each incurs losses measured in billions of dollars.

entries.note: The comparative cash-burn claim explicitly says 'likely.'

entries.test: The March affidavit's compute expenditure and revenue figures would establish whether their ratio is approximately three to one.
Anthropic's disclosed cloud and compute contracts and payments through May 2030 would establish whether its four-year obligations total approximately $380 billion.
entries.note: 'About' preserves the estimated character of the total.

entries.test: Anthropic's cumulative operating expenses over the four years ending around May 2030 would establish whether they reach $20 billion.
entries.note: The source offers an assumed minimum using 'will need'; the proposition substitutes probability language.
He condemns the projections and their reporting; the proposition adds an explicit forecast that they will not come true.

entries.test: Comparable annual loss and gross-margin figures for both labs would establish whether losses increased over time.
entries.note: Falling gross margins alone do not establish increasing absolute losses.

entries.test: Subsequent compute procurement prices, capacity availability and lab margins would show whether shortages force expensive purchases and worsen margins.
entries.note: The forecast includes an asserted causal mechanism but no deadline.
The source explicitly says 'probably.'

entries.test: Anthropic's fundraising disclosures, monthly revenue and cost-of-revenue figures would test whether growth is accompanied by exceptionally high costs.
entries.note: The proposition removes 'allegedly' from the revenue figure and strengthens 'suggests' to 'indicate.'

entries.test: Measured unit costs before and after compute expansion would test whether more compute can make the labs' services cheaper to provide.
entries.note: The passage asserts a cost mechanism; the proposition adds an explicit profitability condition and conflates annualized revenue with annual revenue.

entries.test: New chip deployments and measured service costs would test the hardware prediction, while inference revenue and costs would test Anthropic's current profitability.
entries.note: The source says 'more affordable,' whereas the proposition says 'affordable.' The present profitability component is assessable now.
This imputes private knowledge and motives to CFOs. The proposition also removes 'I think' and strengthens the surrounding tentative account of IPO plans.

entries.test: Enterprise billing records, spending changes and resulting renewal or usage decisions would test whether token billing raises costs and prompts customers to reassess value.
entries.note: The proposition drops 'I believe.' The concrete prediction of sharply rising costs remains testable.

entries.test: Enterprise spending, budget overruns and subsequent renewals or cuts would test whether unsustainable customer spending drives the labs' revenue growth.
entries.note: The extracted claim is Zitron's own causal assertion, separate from the attributed Benioff statement.

entries.test: Enterprise AI budgets, realized quarterly costs and documented reasons for overruns would test the asserted causal chain.
entries.note: 'Nobody actually knows' does not establish that organizations cannot predict costs.
He expresses severe doubt, not a firm denial. The proposition also omits his exception for non-GAAP measurements.

entries.test: Customer token spending, approved budgets and documented overruns would establish whether widespread unusually high spending was occurring.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives 'binge' a concrete budget-overrun reading. The proposition drops 'I think.'

entries.test: Customer contracts, renewal commitments and spending retention data would test whether current token purchases provide evidence of durable recurring revenue.
entries.note: He disputes what present spending indicates rather than explicitly predicting that all such revenue will disappear.

entries.test: Documented company cases linking AI usage mandates to increased defects, maintenance burdens or unreliable code would test the claim.
Zillow's total 2026 AI spending would establish whether it reaches the projected minimum of $7 million.
entries.note: The $7 million trajectory is firm enough to grade; $10 million is only a possibility, not a promised upper bound.

entries.test: Zillow's review-workload measurements and engineering headcount would establish whether additional LLM code review averages about 19 hours per engineer monthly.
Zillow's engineering workflows and documented deployments of the proposed agentic processes would show whether progress had occurred by publication.
entries.note: This is his own endorsed reporting based on sources, rather than a direct quotation.

entries.test: Identified interviewees' organizations and their 2026 token budgets and spending through May would test whether every organization met the stated condition.
entries.note: Undisclosed source identities make verification difficult, not inherently impossible.
The causal explanation says 'might.' The proposition also strengthens data that 'might tell' costs into data that 'would show' them.
He describes an opportunity for manipulation, not an assertion that manipulation occurred.

entries.test: Repeated runs of the same model with identical prompts and context would show whether behavior varies.
entries.note: 'Can' describes an experimentally testable system capability here, rather than an uncertain future possibility.
The source conditionally dismisses budgets as 'bullshit'; the proposition turns the antecedent into an established fact.
'Specifically designed to burn money' is a polemical characterization rather than a concrete design specification.

entries.test: Controlled tests of impossible tasks would show whether generative AI claims it can perform them.
entries.note: He explicitly attributes the 'impression of work' phrase to Mo Bitar while endorsing it. The proposition omits the accompanying flattery claim.

entries.test: Public examples or controlled tests showing LLMs refusing impossible or unsupported requests would falsify the universal claim.
entries.note: Despite emphatic wording, refusal behavior has a straightforward empirical test.
The explanation depends on undefined judgments of leadership incompetence and whether AI is 'good.'

entries.test: Documented generative AI investment, expenditures and losses would test the asserted $1 trillion already burned.
entries.note: The numerical assertion is testable despite the surrounding invective. The proposition adds 'about' to an unqualified figure.
The proposition removes the central accusation of conning customers, softening the original insult.

entries.test: Anthropic's consumer and enterprise revenue and cost disclosures would establish whether it loses money serving both customer groups.
entries.note: The source says Anthropic still loses money when enterprises pay; it does not clearly assert enterprise usage itself has negative margins.
The universal rejection is polemical exaggeration, particularly given his later acknowledgment that people can try and like AI.
This is a sweeping insult about the technology and its intended audience.

entries.test: A documented initial enterprise token-budget cut followed by widespread cuts attributed to that example would test the predicted cascade.
entries.note: The prediction specifies a triggering event but no deadline.
This is an explicit recommendation to shame AI advocates.
